letters.refuse.no_cards: No postcards. The kiosks at the stops have them.
letters.refuse.nobody: Nobody to write to yet: nobody in town knows me.

letters.diary.answer: Wrote to Tonya at White Cape: "{0}"
letters.hint.answer: I can answer Tonya at any postbox
letters.pic.cablecar: The cable car over the cliff
letters.pic.aton: The Aton club on the cliff
letters.phrase.morning: Thank you for saying hello to me in the mornings.
letters.phrase.sea: The sea was quite green today, like bottle glass.
letters.phrase.starlings: Starlings flew over the pier today, thousands, like smoke.
letters.phrase.sunset: Yesterday's sunset was so good I missed my supper.
letters.phrase.thinking: I just thought of you and decided to write.
letters.phrase.weather: May you always have clear weather.
letters.phrase.sun: May the sun shine in at your window.
letters.phrase.tea: Warm tea to you, and long evenings.
letters.reply.kid.1: Hi! Nobody ever sent me a postcard before, and you did. "{0}" is up over my bed. I'll draw you an answer when I can draw starlings.
letters.reply.kid.2: Mum said grown-ups write postcards, and I said one was written to me. Thank you for "{0}"! I showed it to the whole class.
letters.reply.kid.3: Thanks for the postcard! I know that place: "{0}". A gull stole my bun there once. Write again.
letters.reply.teen.1: Wow, a real postcard, stamp and all. "{0}" is cool. I'll write to somebody too, or I'll feel bad.
letters.reply.teen.2: Got the postcard. Looks like an advert at first, then you read it. Thanks. "{0}" is behind the glass in my cupboard now.
letters.reply.teen.3: Hi. The postcard "{0}" came in a day, and I thought the post only went to grannies. See you by the fountain: tell me where you came from.
letters.reply.adult.1: Thank you for the postcard! "{0}" is on my fridge now, next to the bills, and the bills look less frightening for it.
letters.reply.adult.2: Dear neighbour! I don't think I've had a postcard since my student days. "{0}" is a lovely choice. Do drop in if you're on our terrace.
letters.reply.adult.3: Got your postcard "{0}" and went about pleased half the day. At work they asked what had happened. I said: the post. Thank you!
letters.reply.elder.1: Hello, dear boy. Thank you for the postcard "{0}". I've put it in the glass cabinet with the photographs. Let it stand there: it's pretty.
letters.reply.elder.2: Young man! The postcard "{0}" arrived in perfect order. In our day people wrote more often, and they were right to. I shake your hand.
letters.reply.elder.3: Thank you, dear. My neighbour has heard your postcard "{0}" read aloud twice. She wants one too. Come to our bench: I've a sweet for you.
line.letters.thanks.1: Was it you sent me that postcard? Thank you!
line.letters.thanks.2: Got the postcard: it's standing in pride of place.
line.letters.thanks.3: Ah, the amateur postman! Thanks for the card.
line.letters.thanks.4: Thanks for the word. Nobody's written to me for ages.
line.letters.thanks.5: Your postcard came! Now I want to write to somebody too.
line.letters.thanks.6: Thank you for the postcard, my dear.
letters.home.holm.1:
Young man,

Your postcard "{0}" has been taken aboard and stood between the pilot books, where it belongs. The concierge says it was you who wrote the forecast in my log. Your handwriting, forgive me, is a ship's boy's, but the wind is written down right.

V. S. Holm, master mariner
letters.home.holm.2:
Ship's boy,

A second postcard, "{0}", makes a correspondence, and I respect a correspondence. An old friend of mine in Murmansk has played chess with me by postcard for forty years. I offer you a game by post too. My move: e2–e4. You needn't answer with a move: answer with the weather.

V. S. H.
letters.home.holm.invite:
Ship's boy,

I invite you to navy tea. My door, as you know, isn't locked: on board ship we never locked the cabins. Come in the evening: I'll show you how a real watch log is kept and tell you about Biscay in seventy-four. I don't promise sugar; I promise ship's biscuit.

V. S. Holm
letters.shelf.holm: My postcard stands between the pilot books. Next to the one from "K." in Murmansk.
letters.home.okada.1:
My dear viewer,

The postcard "{0}" came with the morning post, and I stood it by my albums at once. A good artist drew it: the light doesn't lie. Asanov downstairs says you looked at my windows long and truly. I'll paint the thousand-and-first with your card on the sill.

L. M. Okada
letters.home.okada.2:
My friend,

A second postcard, "{0}". I read it aloud to Asya. Asya is my wife; she's long gone, but I write to her every evening and, as you see, read her the post. She liked it. She always said postcards are written by people whose summer hasn't ended yet.

L. M.
letters.home.okada.invite:
My friend,

Come by at sunset. I'll set up a second easel and give you a brush: try painting our window just once. It isn't hard. What's hard is stopping at the first. Asanov will pour tea in a glass holder.

L. M. Okada
letters.shelf.okada: My postcard stands by the albums. It seems he's sketched it: the same view in the margin of a pad.
letters.home.singh.1:
Come in!

The postcard "{0}" received, reception excellent. Radio hams answer a contact with a card, so here's mine: "Capsule Tower, Lyudmilovsk. Signal five-nine. Operator Ilmar." Pin it up. You're in my contact log now, number one thousand four hundred and two.

Ilmar, the warden
letters.home.singh.2:
Come in!

A second postcard, "{0}". I report: on Saturday Gunnar was at the Tarelka. Twenty years we talked by radio across one street and never once met. Turns out he's a head taller than me and also drinks his tea without sugar. That's your doing. Over and out, but not quite.

Ilmar
letters.home.singh.invite:
Come in!

I invite you to a night watch on the air. Propagation is best at midnight: sometimes you can hear ships beyond the Skagerrak and fishermen off the Lofotens. Come to the Capsule Tower after eleven. I have a second pair of headphones.

Ilmar
letters.shelf.singh: My postcard stands on the shelf of handbooks, with "QSO No. 1402" pencilled on it.
letters.home.kravets.1:
Hi!

Thanks for "{0}". I stood it on Physics of the Sea, and the book stopped smelling of damp: the card smells of the printer's. I did solve the high-water problem in the end. My answer matched the pier to six minutes. For a first-year, that's a win.

Nora
letters.home.kravets.2:
Hello again!

"{0}" came. Mum sent a parcel from home with cheese and woollen socks and asks whether I have friends here. I answered that people write me postcards. She calmed down. So thank you twice.

Nora
letters.home.kravets.invite:
Hi!

The next full moon brings the highest water of the month. I've worked out the time myself and want to check it on the pier with a tide pole and a torch. I need a witness who won't laugh if I'm wrong. Will you come?

Nora
letters.shelf.kravets: My postcard stands on Physics of the Sea, a tide calculation tucked under it.
letters.home.okafor.1:
Hello, helper!

I've stood the postcard "{0}" on the "For sun" shelf, my best shelf. I found the music from the reel: an old waltz, played, it turns out, by our own sanatorium's band. Half a year I searched the whole world for what was playing round the corner.

Gunnar, UA-Lyudmilovsk-11
letters.home.okafor.2:
Helper,

The postcard "{0}" is the second, so you're a regular correspondent of mine. Ilmar and I go to the Tarelka on Saturdays now. We sit at one table and say nothing, like on the air between sessions. A good sort of nothing.

Gunnar
letters.home.okafor.invite:
Helper,

Saturday at the Tarelka at six. Ilmar, me and, if you come, you. Bring your best news: Ilmar and I have already told each other ours over the radio.

Gunnar
letters.shelf.okafor: My postcard stands among the records on the "For sun" shelf.
letters.home.tadesse.1:
Dear boy,

Thank you for "{0}". Hamish said it lacked a fish, so I drew one in: now a little flounder swims in the corner. Don't be offended: it's professional with me. The card stands in the studio, and the fish in the tank look at it.

V. Tadesse
letters.home.tadesse.2:
My dear correspondent,

A second postcard, "{0}". And we have news: Hamish caught a cod, the first all season, and wouldn't let me paint it: he ate it. He says a still life belongs in the stomach. Fifty years together, and we argue like on our first date.

Valya
letters.home.tadesse.invite:
Dear boy,

Come to the studio and see how I paint water. It's better seen than told. Hamish promises fish soup if they bite and sandwiches if they don't. No need to ring: come in. Don't feed the fish.

V. Tadesse
letters.shelf.tadesse: My postcard stands on the shelf of albums. Somebody has drawn a flounder into its corner.
letters.home.tulegenova.1:
Hello!

Your postcard "{0}" is already in the album for Shira, on a page of its own, with a caption. Shira lives far away, in a city with no sea, and collects other people's towns by postcard. Now she has your view of ours. Thank you!

Priya, flat 5-12
letters.home.tulegenova.2:
Hello again!

Shira has answered! She writes that the card she liked best was the one "with the grey sea in the corners", that is, yours. And the second, "{0}", goes to her in the next letter. Shira sends you her greetings and a question: is it true that here you can see the sun over the sea in the mornings?

Priya
letters.home.tulegenova.invite:
Hello!

Come in the evening, between nine and ten: the blue door on the seventh floor. I'll show you the whole album for Shira, from the first card to yours. There'll be tea with chak-chak: my mother sent some.

Priya
letters.shelf.tulegenova: In the album for Shira my postcard has a page of its own, captioned in small handwriting.
letters.thanks.waxwing:
Hello, observer,

I'm writing because saying it aloud didn't come off. Forty years I walked after waxwings, and this one came to me itself, to my window. I understand it was you who brought it. Thank you. If you see a flock, even one bird, note the day and the place. I'll check the old logs to see whether they're the same ones.

O. Sorokin
letters.thanks.evening_paper:
Hello, sonny!

I read the whole paper, from the weather to the crossword. I didn't solve the crossword: it's all foreign rivers. Vanya says the paper used to come every evening, and everybody in the yard knew who'd read what. Now I'm the only one who knows, and I'll tell everybody. Come for pies: cabbage ones on Thursday.

Nina Korneeva
letters.thanks.crow_gift:
Hi!!!

The crow brought a sweet wrapper to my windowsill today. Mum says it's a present. I put a biscuit crumb out for her too. I'm not afraid of crows any more. Only a tiny bit when they look with one eye. Thank you!!!

Yuki (aged 8)
letters.thanks.fisherman_cheese:
Lad.

The cheese was good. Ate the lot in one evening, with bread, on the porch. My wife would have said you mustn't. No wife now, so you may. Take worms when you need them: the tin's under the boat.

P. Lange
letters.thanks.window_feeder:
Hi, co-author!

Vika has been washing the dishes for five days now and pretends she likes it. And now tits, sparrows and one nuthatch that walks upside down come to the feeder. I keep a count in an exercise book. Come and watch if you like: our kitchen has the best view of the experiment.

Dasha
letters.thanks.magpie_key:
Hi, detective!

Officially: the magpie is acquitted, the key was found on the magnet, I'm to blame. Unofficially: she sits by the workshop every morning now waiting for half a biscuit. I've bought her a whole packet. If anything goes missing, come and we'll investigate together, without suspects this time.

Misha
letters.thanks.painter_views:
Hello!

I've begun painting the town from what you told me. It doesn't come out as the town outside my window but as the one you saw, and that one, I think, is better. The starlings came out like smoke, as you said. If you see anything else worth painting, come and tell me. The legs will be yours again, the brushes mine.

Aya
letters.thanks.first_catch:
Lad.

Look after the spoon: it's a lucky one, I took my first cod on it in sixty-eight. Remember your fish: what it was, where, which wind. There'll be many later, but only one first.

P. Lange
letters.thanks.soda_science:
Esteemed colleague,

I report: the results of your tasting have been repeated in the laboratory with a chromatograph. There are indeed four syrups. The chromatograph confirmed what you determined with your tongue in five minutes. Lev Arkadyevich proposes putting you on the staff. I'm against it: you're too good an instrument for our pay.

G. Zotova
letters.thanks.hot_corn:
My dear,

Ivan never came, but he sent a note with his grandson: "The cob was like in seventy-five. Fish aren't biting much; I'll come when they stop." I've put the note in my purse. Come to the square: corn's half price for you now, and salt's free, as for everyone.

Valentina Guseva
letters.thanks.lab_lunch:
Hi, expert!

On Saturday I went to the Chaika myself. The fish soup really is good, and the dill, in spite of Misha, is too. For the first time in three years I had lunch sitting down and not looking at the measurement log. It turns out there's a point to lunch. Thank you for checking that before me.

Vika
letters.thanks.night_signal:
Esteemed assistant,

I've recalculated. If the light was yours, you stood two metres further left than we agreed, and that explains why it flickered: a pine was in the way. So it probably was you. The experiment counts. We'll do the next one on a clear night, with two torches and no pine.

R. Valiev
letters.thanks.autumn_count:
Colleague,

The count has gone off to the society with two names in the "observer" column. They answered that our patch had been listed as empty for twenty years. Now it isn't. That's not much, but it's true, and in ornithology the truth is worth most of all.

O. Sorokin
letters.invite.generic:
Dear resident,

Lyudmilovsk Town Council invites you to the holiday: {0}. Come yourself and bring your neighbours. There'll be music, treats and good cheer, and we've ordered the weather.

Yours, the Town Council
letters.invite.sea_festival:
Dear resident,

On Saturday it's the holiday: {0}. On the promenade there'll be rowing races, fish soup in big cauldrons and a concert on the pier. The lighthouse keepers will light the lamp earlier than usual, in honour of all those at sea.

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.invite.lantern_night:
Dear resident,

The holiday is coming: {0}. In the evening we'll be sending up sky lanterns on the beach. Write a wish on yours and let it go over the sea. Lanterns and matches are free by the bonfire.

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.invite.first_snow:
Dear resident,

The first snow has fallen, so tomorrow is the holiday: {0}. On the square there'll be hot tea from the samovar, sledging and a snowman contest. Bring your own mittens.

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.invite.winter_fair:
Dear resident,

We invite you to the holiday: {0}. Fair stalls, mulled wine for grown-ups, hot honey drink for all, gingerbread and hand-made tree decorations. Come and choose your presents.

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.invite.new_year:
Dear resident,

The Town Council wishes you joy of the coming holiday: {0}. At midnight there'll be fireworks on the square, and before midnight a tree, music and Grandfather Frost, who has promised not to be late. A happy new year!

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.invite.halloween:
Dear resident,

The holiday is coming: {0}. The children will go from door to door for sweets: keep treats by the door. In the evening on the promenade there'll be lantern pumpkins and scary stories by the bonfire. Not too scary.

Lyudmilovsk Town Council
letters.pen.1.body:
Hello, unknown observer!

My name is Tonya, I'm fourteen, I live at the lighthouse on {0}, and my father is the keeper here. The Friends of Birds bulletin printed a list of young observers, and from Lyudmilovsk there was only one address: the Aton club. I decided it was you.

We have hardly any day left now: the sun shows over the sea for a little while, as if to check that everything's still there. The eiders are gathering in flocks and leaving for the south, maybe for yours. I count them every morning from the lighthouse gallery. Yesterday I counted three hundred and twelve.

Please write and tell me which birds live where you are. I've never been to a warm sea and don't know who flies there.

Tonya Lotsmanova, {0} lighthouse
letters.pen.1.diary: A girl from the lighthouse at White Cape wrote to me: Tonya. She counts eiders and asks which birds we have.
letters.pen.2.body:
Hello!

Your letter came! It went by train, then by car, then on the launch with the post and the bread. Dad said a letter that's come so far deserves tea, and we read it over tea, aloud, twice.

The polar night has begun here. It isn't as frightening as it sounds: in the daytime there's a blue time when everything glows by itself, the snow and the sea. And yesterday there were northern lights, green with a pink edge, moving like a curtain in a draught. The lighthouse lamp looked quite small beside them.

Tell me where you like to walk. Here you can only walk from the lighthouse to the weather station and back, two kilometres, and I know every stone.

Tonya
letters.pen.2.diary: Tonya writes that the polar night has begun there and they had northern lights. She asks where I walk.
letters.pen.3.body:
Hello!

There was a storm for three days. The waves flew over the breakwater, and the lighthouse hummed like a bottle when you blow into it. Dad didn't sleep for two nights, and I carried tea up to him, a hundred and twelve steps. After the storm the snow buntings came to the shore: little, white and brown, as if the snow had learned to fly.

When the ice sets, Dad will take me fishing through a hole. He says you catch navaga here and, if you're lucky, cod. I've never caught anything yet, only dropped a mitten down the hole.

Do you fish? What's caught where you are? Write and tell me which fish you caught yourself.

Tonya
letters.pen.3.diary: Tonya had a three-day storm, and snow buntings came after it. She asks what fish I've caught.
letters.pen.4.body:
Hello!

I have a friend. His name is Captain, and he's a raven. He lives on the roof of the weather station and every morning flies over to the lighthouse to check whether anything's left from breakfast. At first he only took bread if I stepped ten paces away. Then five. Yesterday he took a rusk straight off my mitten and looked at me as if he had tamed me, not I him.

Dad says ravens remember faces for many years. So Captain will remember me even when I grow up and go away to study.

Do you have a friend among the birds? Does anybody take food from your hand?

Tonya
letters.pen.4.diary: Tonya has made friends with a raven called Captain: he takes a rusk from her mitten. She asks if I have a friend among the birds.
letters.pen.5.body:
Hello!

A miracle happened: an ivory gull came to the lighthouse. Completely white, like porcelain, with black feet. Dad said there are very few of them left, and in thirty years at the lighthouse he's seen one four times. She sat on the gallery rail for about three minutes, looked at the lamp and flew off into the dark. I didn't even have time to call Dad a second time.

Now I go out on the gallery every hour, though I know she won't come back. Maybe that's how people become ornithologists: you see something once and then wait all your life.

Who have you seen that's new? It seems to me you have someone new every day.

Tonya
letters.pen.5.diary: An ivory gull came to Tonya's lighthouse: her father has seen one only four times. Tonya asks who I've seen that's new.
letters.pen.6.body:
Hello!

I'm drawing a map of our cape. A real one, with a scale and a wind rose, like the one on Dad's wall. I've marked the lighthouse, the weather station, Seal Rock, the stream that sings in summer and is silent in winter, and the place where Captain hides his treasures: he has a jar lid there, a spoon and a blue button.

When the map's ready I'll send you a copy. And you send me your place, the best one, and I'll draw it in the margin with an arrow: "Lyudmilovsk, that way". Then my map will have two ends of the earth, ours and yours.

Tonya
letters.pen.6.diary: Tonya is drawing a map of her cape and wants to draw my best place in the margin.
letters.pen.7.body:
Hello!

The map is ready, and I'm sending you a copy. I drew your place in the margin, where the map's north ends and everything else begins.

It's the darkest week of the year here. I go to school by radio: the teacher reads the lesson from the mainland, and we, four children from different stations, answer in turn. It's hard to hear, but fun. Dad says it'll soon turn towards the light, and that he feels it in his knees before he sees it.

I'm keeping a list of the winter's birds. So far I have nine species. Send me one more, yours, and I'll write it in on a line of its own: "seen by my friend in the south".

Tonya
letters.pen.7.diary: Tonya sent a copy of her map, with my place in the margin. She's keeping a list of winter birds and asks for one more, mine.
letters.pen.8.body:
Hello, my friend in the south!

Your bird is written into the list as the tenth, on a line of its own, as I promised.

Dad says the sun will come back very soon. On the day it looks out from beyond the sea, I'll climb to the very top of the lighthouse, to the lamp, and wave your way. I looked on the map: it's right over Seal Rock and on, far away, across the whole country. If the sun shines in at your window that day, know that it's me waving.

In spring the eiders will come back. Count them where you are when they fly north, and I'll count them here when they arrive. That way we'll know how many made it. Write to me. Always write.

Your Tonya, {0} lighthouse

P.S. There's a feather of Captain's in the envelope. He said I could.
letters.pen.8.diary: Tonya writes: when the sun comes back to them, she'll climb up to the lighthouse lamp and wave my way. Her raven's feather is in the envelope.
letters.pen.nudge:
Hello!

Did you get my letter? Our post comes when it likes: the launch waits for the weather, the weather waits for the wind. If you didn't get it, I'll write again. If you did, just write two words, and I'll know you're there.

Tonya
letters.pen.ack.bird.1: You write that you saw this: {0}! I found it in Dad's field guide and circled it in pencil. We don't have them here; now I'll know they're there with you.
letters.pen.ack.bird.2: I told Captain about the bird you saw ({0}). He pretended not to care, but he listened.
letters.pen.ack.fish.1: Your fish, {0}, is a real catch! Dad said well done and that a first fish must go in the log. I wrote yours in mine.
letters.pen.ack.fish.2: You caught a fish: {0}. And I've only caught a mitten so far. But the ice has nearly set, so wait for news.
letters.pen.ack.place.1: I imagined your place: {0}. I shut my eyes and imagined the smell of the sea there, only warm. I almost managed it.
letters.pen.ack.place.2: Your place ({0}) is on my map now too, in the margin, with an arrow.
letters.pen.ack.friend.1: So you have a winged friend too: {0}! When I read it to Captain, he cawed twice. I think that means "respect".
letters.pen.ack.friend.2: Your friend, {0}, eats from your palm. So you and I have the same kind of hands: they're trusted.
letters.pen.ack.none.1: You write that nothing special has happened yet. But I think every day is special where you are: you're just used to it.
letters.pen.ack.none.2: Thank you for answering even when there's nothing to tell. That matters too: it means the letter got there.
letters.pen.answer.bird: I saw a bird: {0}. I crept up quite close and watched through the binoculars for a long time.
letters.pen.answer.fish: I caught a fish: {0}! Myself, with a rod, on the pier.
letters.pen.answer.place: My best place: {0}. You'd like it there.
letters.pen.answer.friend: I have a winged friend: {0}. It eats from my palm and comes when I call.
letters.pen.answer.none: Nothing special yet. But I'm keeping my eyes open and will write for sure.
